title: Optimal regret for private stochastic online learning
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal expected pseudo-regret \(R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\) for pure differentially private stochastic full-information online learning. The domain is integers \(K\ge2\), \(T\ge1\), and real parameters \(\varepsilon>0\), \(0<\Delta\le1\). For independent loss distributions \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) on \([0,1]\), let \(\mu_j=\mathbb E_{P_j}[L]\); require a unique minimizer \(j^{*}\) and \(\mu_j-\mu_{j^{*}}\ge\Delta\) for every \(j\ne j^{*}\). At round \(t\), select \(I_t\in[K]\) using only earlier observations and private randomness, incur loss \(L_{I_t,t}\), and then observe the entire vector \(L_t\), where all \(L_{j,t}\sim P_j\) are independent across actions and rounds. Put \[R^{*}(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)=\inf_A\sup_{(P_1,\ldots,P_K)}\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\mu_{I_t}-\mu_{j^{*}})\right],\] where the supremum ranges over the promised product distributions and the infimum over the causal \(\varepsilon\)-private strategies defined below. The requested rate retains every dependence on \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\), including logarithmic factors and the small-horizon regime.
why: This asks how protecting one round of observations changes the achievable accuracy of sequential decisions even when the environment is stationary and all actions are observed. A sharp rate would identify the statistical price of pure privacy and whether the remaining dependence on the number of actions is necessary.
status_note: The original question is open in Hu–Mehta 2024; the checked final ALT 2026 paper explicitly reports only a partial solution and retains a logarithmic stochastic gap. No matching complete rate was found in the bounded later-work search on 15 September 2026. This formulation is a stated minimax interpretation of the original gap-dependent question.

progress.text: Hu and Mehta pose the matching-order pure-privacy problem and explain why unequal suboptimality gaps leave uncertainty about the best privacy term.
Published ALT 2026 Theorem 3 gives a horizon-independent stochastic upper bound with privacy contribution \(\log^{2}K/\varepsilon\); §4 resolves its deterministic-loss comparison problem only.

sentences: A learner repeatedly chooses an action and then observes the losses of every action.
The losses are independent draws from fixed unknown distributions, and one action has strictly smallest mean loss.
The card asks for matching-order expected pseudo-regret under pure privacy protecting one entire round of observations.
A published 2026 upper bound removes the time-horizon factor but leaves a logarithmic gap in the number of actions.
A solution must identify the rate throughout the stated parameter domain and certify both achievable guarantees and unavoidable loss in Lean.

definitions: \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\). The public parameters are \(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta\); the gap bound \(\Delta\) is a promise supplied to the strategy, while the distributions, their means, and the best-action index are unknown. This is the minimax interpretation of the source's gap-dependent optimal-rate question: the worst case is over all instances whose minimum gap is at least the supplied threshold, rather than one specified vector of means. A strategy is a family of Borel-measurable probability kernels for \(I_t\), given the public parameters, earlier actions, and earlier full loss vectors. It may retain arbitrary private state and use correlated internal randomness; equivalently use the conditional kernels of its observable history. No running-time, memory, or properness restriction is imposed. The output available to a privacy observer is the complete action sequence, not the privately observed losses. For every pair of deterministic sequences \(s,s'\in([0,1]^K)^T\) differing in at most one entire loss vector, and every event \(E\subseteq[K]^T\), require \[\Pr[A(s)\in E]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[A(s')\in E].\] This requirement applies to all loss sequences, including nonstochastic ones, and has no additive privacy slack. Its prefix versions follow by projection. The utility expectation includes both the stochastic losses and the strategy's independent initial randomness. Pseudo-regret compares against the smallest expected loss, not the smallest realized cumulative loss. The first action is selected before any losses are revealed. There is no adversarial dependence of later losses on released actions. Infima need not be attained; approaching strategies qualify.
answer_criterion: Supply a nonnegative rate function \(B(K,T,\varepsilon,\Delta)\), an explicit family of admissible private strategies, and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), with a Lean-checked proof that \(cB\le R^{*}\le CB\) throughout the stated domain. The upper bound must hold for every promised product distribution; the lower bound must apply to every causal private strategy and allow a worst-case promised distribution. If an infimum is not attained, certify arbitrarily close upper bounds instead of requiring an optimal strategy. Constants cannot depend on any of the four parameters. A bound only for deterministic losses, bandit feedback, approximate privacy, or only one side of the rate does not meet this criterion. This is asymptotic precision in unnormalized cumulative pseudo-regret, not an additive \(1/100\) approximation.

source_formulation.text: Determine matching-order bounds for gap-dependent pseudo-regret under pure differential privacy in stochastic full-information decision-theoretic online learning.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: After each decision, the learner sees how every action performed. This makes the problem different from a bandit problem, where it sees only the chosen action. In a stationary environment, the mean-loss gaps measure how much evidence separates the best action from its competitors. The total error from exploring those competitors can remain bounded as the number of rounds grows.

Privacy treats one complete observed loss vector as one record and protects the joint distribution of all released actions. Protecting each action separately would not suffice: an observer can combine decisions across many rounds. Pure privacy also excludes a small additive exceptional-event term, which is explicitly outside the source question.

The 2024 paper compares an upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K\log T/\varepsilon)\) with a long-horizon lower scale \(\Omega(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log K/\varepsilon)\). Its authors expressly do not conjecture that this lower scale is optimal. Those displayed rates describe the nontrivial parameter regime; a lower bound independent of \(T\) cannot hold for arbitrarily short horizons because regret is at most \(T\).

Wu and Wang prove the improved stochastic upper bound \(O(\log K/\Delta_{\min}+\log^{2}K/\varepsilon)\). It removes dependence on \(T\) from the gap-dependent upper bound. A logarithmic factor in \(K\) remains between the stated upper and lower privacy terms. Their matching \(\Theta(\log K/\varepsilon)\) result applies to the separate model with deterministic loss vectors and does not settle the stochastic question.

The card makes the minimax quantifier convention explicit by supplying a lower gap promise \(\Delta\) and retaining finite \(T\). An upper bound using only the actual minimum gap also applies to this promise class. Sharp finite-horizon transitions and boundary gaps are part of the stated rate; the displayed long-horizon literature bounds are not claimed uniformly tight there.
